## The idea

A wrong transcription often sounds vaguely wrong long before the faulty event
is visible. Validation turns that feeling into a smaller search space. Assert
the duration of every bar. Assert a plausible range. Flag melodic leaps larger
than an octave for human review. These checks do not prove the notes are right,
but they remove whole families of mistakes.

Most rhythmic faults I make come from a missing tie, a rest counted twice, or a
dotted value entered without its dot. A bar-total failure catches all three.
Pitch range and leap checks are weaker because music can exceed them on
purpose. Treat those as warnings rather than automatic corrections.

After the structural checks, loop one suspicious bar against the source. A
four-second comparison reveals more than replaying the whole minute and hoping
to notice the fault on the next pass.

## Run this

The score uses one array per bar. Each event has a note, local start, and
duration. The validator raises on bad meter and prints review messages for
unusual pitch movement.

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 80
use_synth :piano

bars = [
  [
    {note: 60, start: 0.0, duration: 1.0},
    {note: 62, start: 1.0, duration: 1.0},
    {note: 64, start: 2.0, duration: 2.0}
  ],
  [
    {note: 67, start: 0.0, duration: 1.0},
    {note: 79, start: 1.0, duration: 1.0}, # octave leap: review
    {note: 76, start: 2.0, duration: 2.0}
  ]
]

define :validate_bar do |events, expected_beats|
  total = events.map { |event| event[:duration] }.sum
  raise "bar totals #{total}, expected #{expected_beats}" unless total == expected_beats

  events.each_cons(2) do |left, right|
    leap = (right[:note] - left[:note]).abs
    puts "REVIEW leap of #{leap} semitones" if leap >= 12
  end
end

define :play_events do |events|
  events.each do |event|
    play event[:note], release: event[:duration] * 0.8
    sleep event[:duration]
  end
end

bars.each do |bar|
  validate_bar bar, 4.0
  play_events bar
end
```

Both bars occupy four beats. The log flags the octave in bar 2, and the sound
makes that event easy to locate. The warning does not say the leap is wrong.

## Change one thing

1. Change the final duration in bar 1 from 2.0 to 1.5. Run again. Playback stops
   at the assertion, before a malformed bar can contaminate later review.
2. Restore the duration and change note 79 to 80. The range rises and the leap
   becomes thirteen semitones. Add a range warning for notes below 48 or above
   84, then decide whether this event needs one or two review messages.
3. Replace bars.each with three repetitions of play_events bars[1]. Compare
   that short loop with the same source interval. Listen first for attack time,
   then pitch, then release.

## Why it works

Assertions encode invariants. In 4/4, a complete bar normally accounts for four
beats, including rests and tied continuations. If the representation stores
rests separately, include them in the total. If a pickup is shorter, give that
bar an explicit expected length. Avoid weakening the assertion globally to
accommodate one exception.

Absolute event starts support another check: sort events by start, reject
negative durations, and detect overlaps that the source does not mark. A
sequential array is easier to type, while start times are easier to compare
against a timeline. Convert between them in one helper rather than maintaining
two hand-edited copies.

Warnings are evidence for manual review. A leap over an octave can be correct,
especially in arpeggiated music. Range limits depend on instrument, voice, and
transposition. The software narrows attention; the source settles the claim.

The milestone for this part is a thirty-to-sixty-second melody with source
reference, bar-level data, validation helpers, and a separate expressive
renderer. Ruby syntax checks can inspect the program, but the sound still
requires auditioning in Sonic Pi.

## Take it further

Add a validation report to the transcription from Lesson 45. It must list each
bar total, overall note range, leaps of twelve semitones or more, and every
REVIEW marker. Then choose one suspicious bar and create a temporary three-pass
loop: neutral rhythm, strict pitch, expressive rendering. The target is a clean
report with every surviving warning explained in a comment rather than deleted
to make the output quiet.
